b2-LGF-C:
Mitochondrial fuels (glutamine, butyrate, TCA intermediates): your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, right there in the gut, to keep the tight junctions tight. If the cells lining your small intestine (enterocytes) or large intestine (colonocytes) don't get the fuels their mitochondria prefer, the barrier physically falls apart and lets lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and endotoxins leak into your bloodstream.
L-Glutamine (watch Dr. Rhonda vid) is the main fuel for enterocytes, and for activated immune cells. It skips the complicated digestive steps and gets turned straight into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG) inside the mitochondria, which powers the citric acid cycle. That quick energy hit drives the repair of the gut lining and stops LPS from getting through.
5g a day is the baseline, to counter the breakdown of the gut lining you get from high-intensity or high-volume training like CrossFit or intense cardio. Work up to 10-30g a day during acute immune exposure or high systemic stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's/Colitis).
But fast-growing cancer cells can grab glutamine too, to fuel their growth, so don't work up to the high doses if you have an active colon or liver cancer (the liver sees it first, since it comes through the portal vein).
Butyrate and SCFAs: the small intestine runs on glutamine, but the large intestine runs on short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate. You get those from fermenting raw resistant starch, or from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt, and they fuel the colonocytes, lock down the lower gut barrier and suppress inflammatory signals.
TCA cycle intermediates (malic and citric acid): malate and citrate feed into the same mitochondrial energy pathways as glutamine. So clean sour stuff like organic malic acid, tart cherries or green apples is another quick fuel for the cells lining your gut, and speeds up healing of the lining from a different biochemical angle.
b2-ST1-C:
Optional Ready-Made Gut Stacks
I don't think there's one supplement stack that heals everyone's gut. The order still matters: fix the digestion mechanics first, then reset diet and motility, and only go to antimicrobial or anti-parasite protocols if your symptoms are still there.
But some people want a ready-made starting point instead of buying everything separately. For a general "repair and rebuild" stack, I'd want it to cover three things: something for the microbiome (a probiotic or probiotic system you tolerate well), something for prebiotics and butyrate (that helps you make short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate), and something to repair the barrier, nutrients for the gut lining like glutamine, zinc carnosine, colostrum, mucosal-support herbs or similar.
b2-ST2-C:
Gemini suggested these kits, but so far they're the best ones I've seen, tho I haven't used them myself, so check the reviews. Microbiome Labs Total Gut Restoration is the best general stack, because it has probiotic, prebiotic and mucosal-support parts. If it's more of a leaky gut thing, Dr. Ruscio's Leaky Gut Support Kit is a reasonable option. And Designs for Health GI Revive is one of the more complete single formulas for the gut lining, but it's a repair product, not a whole gut protocol by itself.
I wouldn't use the general "gut cleanse" stacks, the ones built around oregano oil, wormwood, black walnut, berberine or other antimicrobial herbs, as a starting point for everyone. Those come later, when there's a stronger reason to suspect overgrowth, parasites, H. pylori or some other specific problem. (For H. pylori my own advice is different, since berberine works well for it: see Parasites, above.)
Start with low doses, especially of prebiotics, resistant starch, butyrate-support products and probiotics. And if you have severe pain, GI bleeding, fever, dehydration, rapid weight loss, an active IBD flare, cancer, immune suppression, pregnancy or a complex medical condition, work with a qualified clinician instead of stacking supplements on your own.
